<reason>Both sides were sharp and the clash was genuine. CON built an ingenious case: "genuinely necessary" is indeterminate ex ante, the degree is a defensible proxy that arose because better tests were legally perilous, and removing it shifts weight to referrals and interview polish that are more wealth-wired. But PRO neutralized the two load-bearing pieces. On equity, PRO repeatedly showed the degree is an additional gate stacked before the interview, that graduates keep their diploma under the motion (it stops being required, not considered), and that the "credential a stranger can acquire alone" still costs four years and money—CON's "a scholarship exists" reply was thin. On indeterminacy, PRO gave a usable test ("can the person do the work without the paper?") backed by the everyday practice of degree-free postings; CON's licensing/cheap-error answer was its best moment but conceded the question is answerable in principle. CON's "complied if honest" dilemma was rhetorically effective but PRO's "don't ask about age" analogy adequately explained how a normative standard changes behavior without a tribunal, and CON's argument drifted toward "the motion is empty" rather than "the motion is wrong." PRO's weighing—CON never claims necessity, defends only odds-shifting, against a filter discarding two-thirds of adults—remained undisputed at the close. PRO was clipped three times and mislabeled references, a real execution cost, but CON was also clipped and the substance still favored PRO.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A2 in Rebuttal 2 [A4.4–A4.6]: dismantling CON's "degree vs interview" framing by noting graduates are interviewed too, so the degree only removes the poor candidate before the polish contest, and that "no legible track record" better describes the 22-year-old graduate than the worker employed since eighteen. CON's "interview is the constant" reply did not restore the equity reversal.</best_rebuttal>
